analysis.one_liner: Requires health insurers to cover routine care costs for cancer patients in clinical trials.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to three House committees and subcommittees in May 2003 but never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the 108th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required group health plans and individual health insurers to cover the routine patient care costs of people with cancer who enroll in federally approved clinical trials. Plans could not deny someone a trial, refuse to pay the routine costs, or discriminate against them for participating. The insurers would not have had to pay for the experimental drug itself, which trial sponsors typically provide free. The bill also directed federal agencies to study the cost of extending the same rule to other serious diseases.
analysis.who_benefits: People with cancer who are covered by a group or individual health plan and who are eligible for an approved clinical trial. Many insurers at the time refused to pay routine care costs associated with trials, which could leave patients to pay out of pocket or forgo promising research treatments. The bill also protected trial participants from being penalized by their plan for joining a trial.

how_it_helps.text: Group health plans and insurers could not deny an eligible cancer patient participation in an approved clinical trial or deny, limit, or add conditions to coverage of the routine patient care costs connected to it.
Plans could not discriminate against a patient because of their participation in a clinical trial.

The rules would apply to individual-market insurance as well as employer group plans, effective for plan years starting on or after January 1, 2004, with a delay for plans governed by existing collective bargaining agreements.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurance plans and issuers, which would bear the cost of routine care for trial participants; those costs would ultimately be passed to employers and policyholders through premiums. The bill directed agencies to report to Congress on the incremental cost to group health plans by January 2007.

drawbacks.text: Plans would pay more: they must cover routine patient costs such as conventional care, administration and monitoring of the investigational treatment, and care for complications, which would add to premiums borne by employers and enrollees.

The mandate was limited to federally approved trials and did not require plans to pay for the investigational drug or device itself, so the most expensive items would still be covered by research sponsors rather than insurance.
The bill did not address uninsured cancer patients, who would get no help from this coverage mandate.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The protection is real and targeted: it costs insurers mainly the routine care these patients would often need anyway, and it keeps research sponsors paying for the experimental agents. Studies of similar mandates (not in this record) have generally found modest cost, and the bill itself ordered a federal cost study before extending the rule to other diseases. The design is careful, but its scope is narrow and it does nothing for the uninsured.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees after referral, was sent to their health subcommittees, and no hearing or vote ever happened before Congress expired.

narrative.text: Representative Deborah Pryce of Ohio, with three original cosponsors from both parties, introduced the bill on May 7, 2003.
It was referred to three committees: Energy and Commerce, Education and the Workforce, and Ways and Means.
Within three weeks, the bill was sent down to the Health subcommittees of Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means, and to the Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee of Education and the Workforce.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed; the last recorded action was the subcommittee referrals in May 2003, and the bill died when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and self-insured employers were better off because the bill never advanced, since they avoided a mandate to cover routine care costs for cancer patients in trials. Insured cancer patients hoping for trial coverage were left where they started.

for.name: Rep. Deborah Pryce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Access to Cancer Clinical Trials Act of 2003 on May 7, 2003.

for.name: Reps. Sue Myrick, Lois Capps, and Steve Israel
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: House committee chairs (Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce)
against.role: Committee chairs of the three committees of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a hearing or markup after referral; the only actions ever taken were the referrals and subcommittee assignments in May 2003.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor at any point in the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Republican and drew cosponsors from both parties (1 Republican and 5 Democrats among its six cosponsors), so the split was not partisan; it simply never got far enough for a vote that would have revealed one.

industries.note: The bill would have mandated that group and individual plans cover the routine care costs of cancer patients in approved trials and barred plans from denying or penalizing trial participation. Insurers' interest in avoiding those added costs ran directly against patients' access to trials.

industries.industry: Cancer clinical trial sponsors and drug makers
industries.note: By requiring insurers to pick up routine care costs, the bill would make it easier to recruit patients into federally approved cancer trials, which trial sponsors (NIH-funded centers and drug companies testing investigational agents) depend on. Patients got access at the same time, so the interests ran together.
ERISA plans would face the same coverage mandate, an added benefits cost for employers, offset for patients by access to trials.
